questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Infarction of blood vessels supplying the cerebral cortex most commonly results in:
questions.explanation: Cerebral cortical infarction typically causes upper motor neuron lesions resulting in spastic paralysis, as the corticospinal tract controls voluntary movement and its interruption leads to hypertonia and hyperreflexia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In syringomyelia, sensory loss typically follows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which brain structure is typically damaged in left‑sided hemiballismus?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus results from damage to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, causing violent flinging movements of the opposite side of the body.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Fibers from the cerebral cortex to the corpus striatum release which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: The corticostriatal pathway uses glutamate as its neurotransmitter, providing excitatory input from the cerebral cortex to the corpus striatum (caudate and putamen).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Static tremor is caused by which mechanism in the basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: Static (resting) tremor in Parkinson's disease results from oscillatory activity between the globus pallidus interna and subthalamic nucleus due to loss of dopamine.
options: Loss of dopamine in substantia nigra
Oscillation between GPi and subthalamic nucleus

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How does dopamine act on the basal ganglia motor pathways?
questions.explanation: D1 receptors in the direct pathway are excitatory; dopamine binding to D1 receptors stimulates the direct pathway which ultimately facilitates movement via reduced GPi activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Glutamate is secreted by:
questions.explanation: Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which function is performed by the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum corrects movements on the same side of the body through its deep cerebellar nuclei and their projections to the thalamus and motor cortex.
options: Correct movement on the same side of the body
Initiation of voluntary movement on the same side
Coordination of opposite side limb movements

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which statement about climbing fibers is correct?
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers originate from the inferior olivary nucleus, form powerful excitatory synapses on Purkinje cells, each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber, and they play a role in motor learning.
options: They originate from the inferior olivary nucleus
They form powerful excitatory synapses on Purkinje cells
Each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber
They play a role in motor learning

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which deficit is most characteristic of a cerebellar lesion?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesions characteristically impair motor learning (adaptation of movements), as the cerebellum is essential for procedural memory and motor skill acquisition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which structure is primarily responsible for the damping action that prevents tremors during voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is responsible for the damping action that prevents overshoot and tremors during voluntary movements through its feedback loops.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which function is primarily associated with the flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is primarily concerned with equilibrium and balance, receiving input from the vestibular apparatus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which clinical sign is characteristic of an ipsilateral cerebellar lesion?
questions.explanation: Ipsilateral cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia due to loss of the cerebellum's facilitatory influence on alpha motor neurons and reduced gamma motor activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Tremors present during voluntary movement and reduced during sleep indicate which condition?
questions.explanation: Intention tremor (present during voluntary movement, reduced during sleep) is characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction, as opposed to resting tremor seen in basal ganglia disorders.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which deficit is specifically associated with a lesion affecting climbing fibers of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: Climbing fiber lesions specifically impair motor learning (adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex), as these fibers from the inferior olive encode error signals for cerebellar plasticity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzymatic change explains the slow rate of glycolysis in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons have reduced PFK-2/FBPase3 activity, resulting in low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, which inhibits glycolysis and makes neurons dependent on oxidative metabolism.
options: High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which inhibits formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of hexokinase with decreased intracellular glucose
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate (variant)
High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which stimulates formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During excessive exercise, which substance serves as an energy source for neurons?
questions.explanation: During excessive exercise, lactate produced by astrocytes serves as an energy source for neurons through the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which statement about ketone bodies is correct?
questions.explanation: Ketone bodies are not a major energy source in the well-fed state; the brain preferentially uses glucose. They become important during starvation when glucose is scarce.
options: Main energy source for the brain
Main energy source for the liver during starvation
Not a major source of energy in well‑fed state

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During starvation, which of the following occurs?
questions.explanation: During starvation, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) as an alternative fuel when glucose availability decreases.
options: Ketone bodies are utilized in liver
Ketone bodies are utilized in brain
Fatty acids are utilized in brain
Amino acids are utilized in brain

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is absent in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons lack PFK2/FBPase3 (the bifunctional enzyme that produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate), resulting in low glycolytic rate and dependence on oxidative metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which laboratory finding is used as a marker for carcinoid tumor?
questions.explanation: 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main metabolite of serotonin, is elevated in urine and used as a marker for carcinoid tumors that secrete serotonin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors throughout the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which substance acts as an antioxidant in astrocytes by forming reduced glutathione?
questions.explanation: NADPH in astrocytes provides reducing equivalents for the glutathione reductase system, converting GSSG to reduced glutathione (GSH) to combat oxidative stress.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In pheochromocytoma, which metabolite is typically increased in urine?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumor) causes elevated urinary VMA (vanillylmandelic acid), the main metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid is the precursor of serotonin?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is the precursor amino acid for serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) synthesis via the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which drug prevents the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, preventing conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS, allowing more levodopa to reach the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which glucose transporter is present on astrocytes?
questions.explanation: GLUT1 is the glucose transporter predominantly expressed on astrocytes and the blood-brain barrier, facilitating glucose entry into the CNS.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which is the rate‑limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase (converting tyrosine to L-DOPA) is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis and requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the final disposal form of the amino group in the human body?
questions.explanation: Urea is the final disposal form of amino groups in humans, produced in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted in urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which amino acid becomes essential?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency prevents citrulline formation from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate; arginine becomes essential since the urea cycle cannot complete without it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The nitrogen atoms of urea are derived from which sources?
questions.explanation: Urea contains two nitrogen atoms: one from ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase reaction).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acids are responsible for the characteristic burned sugar odor of urine in maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate in maple syrup urine disease due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A month‑old baby’s urine has a sweet, burnt sugar smell. Elevated leucine, isoleucine, valine. Which enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which reaction is impaired in thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; its deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In phenylketonuria, which substance accumulates in the blood?
questions.explanation: PKU results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing accumulation of phenylalanine which is neurotoxic and leads to intellectual disability if untreated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which disease and metabolite pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is correctly matched with phenylpyruvate; the disease causes phenylalanine accumulation and its transamination products (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate) are excreted.
options: Maple syrup urine disease and isolysine
Maple syrup urine disease and lysine
Maple syrup urine disease and glycine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In phenylketonuria, deficiency of which substance occurs?
questions.explanation: In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency leads to inability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, resulting in tyrosine deficiency and catecholamine synthesis impairment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 55‑year‑old chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ataxia, and memory impairment. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in chronic alcoholics presents with the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and memory impairment due to thiamine (B1) deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the same patient (alcoholic, confusion, ataxia), which enzyme is affected?
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; its deficiency impairs this enzyme causing neurological dysfunction in Wernicke-Korsakoff.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin is required for one‑carbon transfer reactions involved in nucleotide synthesis?
questions.explanation: Folic acid (as N5, N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate) provides one-carbon units for thymidylate synthase and purine synthesis reactions in nucleotide biosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Impairment of oxidative decarboxylation leads to inability to utilize glucose due to deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for oxidative decarboxylation reactions catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic diarrhea, cognitive decline, and photosensitive skin rash. Which supplement?
questions.explanation: The triad of diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis (photosensitive rash) is classic for pellagra caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is neurologically affected by folic acid status – folic acid can mask hematological signs but not prevent neurological damage?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord; folic acid can mask the anemia but does not prevent neurological progression.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which biochemical process is inhibited by sulfonamides?
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis in bacteria (humans obtain folate from diet, not synthesis).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamins are directly required for the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine?
questions.explanation: Homocysteine remethylation to methionine requires methyltetrahydrofolate (from folic acid) as methyl donor and methionine synthase (which needs B12).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which reaction uses methyltetrahydrofolate as a cofactor?
questions.explanation: Methyltetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which acts as a coenzyme for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases?
questions.explanation: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the essential cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases including phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The conversion of which requires vitamin B12 and folic acid?
questions.explanation: Homocysteine to methionine conversion requires both vitamin B12 (as methylcobalamin) and folic acid (as methyltetrahydrofolate) for the methionine synthase reaction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which statement is true regarding neuroglia?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes perform gliosis (reactive astrogliosis) in response to CNS injury, forming glial scars; they also maintain the blood-brain barrier and ion balance.
options: Schwann cells are found in the CNS
Ependymal cells form nodes of Ranvier

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which statement is true regarding the layers of the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger (optic radiation fibers) is found in the inner granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex, while the inner band is in layer V.
options: The outer band of Baillarger is present in the inner granular layer
The inner band of Baillarger is present in the molecular layer
The molecular layer contains large pyramidal cells
The inner granular layer lacks stellate cells
The multiform layer is the most superficial layer

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which correctly describes a feature of Pacinian corpuscles compared to Meissner corpuscles?
questions.explanation: In Pacinian corpuscles, the afferent fiber passes axially through the center, while in Meissner corpuscles the nerve fiber has a coiled (tortuous) course between lamellar cells.
options: Pacinian detect light touch, Meissner detect vibration
Pacinian are mainly in non‑hairy skin, Meissner in hairy skin
Pacinian are in epidermis, Meissner in dermis
Pacinian detect temperature, Meissner detect pain
Pacinian have fibers that pass axially through the corpuscle, Meissner fibers are coiled

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which receptors provide the sense of movement and position of the body?
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors) provide information about body position, movement, and limb location in space.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which feature characterizes the nerve ending in a Meissner’s corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The nerve fiber in Meissner's corpuscle has a characteristic tortuous (coiled) course between the lamellar cells, unlike the straight axial course in Pacinian corpuscles.
options: Myelinated afferent fiber enters the base of the corpuscle

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which sensation is primarily detected by Meissner’s corpuscles?
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that detect crude touch and tactile discrimination, particularly in glabrous skin.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic onion-like lamellar structure located in dermis and deeper tissues.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which feature is common to both free nerve endings and Merkel’s discs?
questions.explanation: Both free nerve endings and Merkel's discs are found in the epidermis; free nerve endings detect pain and temperature while Merkel discs detect light touch.
options: They are the most numerous sensory receptors in the body
Found in the epidermis of the skin
Arise from subepidermal plexus of nerves

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which type of receptor is found in the cornea?
questions.explanation: The cornea contains abundant free nerve endings (no specific encapsulated receptors) making it extremely sensitive to pain and touch.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which sensory receptors penetrate the epidermis?
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings and Merkel discs both penetrate the epidermis; free nerve endings respond to pain/temperature while Merkel discs mediate light touch.
options: Free nerve endings and Merkel discs
Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs
Krause end bulbs and Ruffini endings

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Regarding the cervical spinal cord, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) is located in lamina II of the spinal cord gray matter and processes pain and temperature sensations.
options: Substantia gelatinosa receives mostly motor input
Substantia gelatinosa is located in lamina II
Clarke’s nucleus is located in lamina VI
Clarke’s nucleus is found in all cervical segments
Retropostero‑lateral column of cervical segments supplies the distal part of the lower limb

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which statement about Clarke’s nucleus is correct?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is present at all thoracic levels (T1-L2) and is the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
options: Clarke’s nucleus is present at all levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all cervical levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all thoracic levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all lumbar levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all sacral levels

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which structure is found in the cervical segment (internal structures of spinal cord)?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus is found in lamina VII (intermediate gray matter) at cervical levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
options: Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII grey matter
Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII white matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII grey matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII white matter
Substantia gelatinosa in lamina VII grey matter

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which structure is found in lamina I of the spinal cord gray matter?
questions.explanation: The posteromarginal nucleus is located in lamina I of the spinal cord and receives pain and temperature afferents from the periphery.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which type of neuron forms synaptic junctions with intrafusal muscle fibers within a muscle spindle?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles, regulating spindle sensitivity and the stretch reflex loop.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following nuclei has motor function?
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nucleus (in the anterior horn) has motor function, containing motor neuron pools for axial and proximal limb muscles.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which opioid is a long‑acting, pure agonist associated with milder withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Methadone is a long-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in opioid maintenance therapy, producing milder withdrawal due to its slow dissociation from receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is found unconscious with pinpoint pupils and hypothermia, suspected heroin intoxication. Which drug should be administered?
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses heroin intoxication by blocking mu-opioid receptors, restoring respiratory drive.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which opioid acts as a partial agonist at the μ receptor and is used in opioid dependence management?
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa antagonist, producing ceiling effects on respiratory depression and milder withdrawal.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An alcoholic patient shows dependence related to activation of opioid receptors. Which drug is used for treatment?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence by blocking opioid receptors involved in reward pathways.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug can be used to manage fentanyl intoxication?
questions.explanation: Naloxone, like naltrexone, is an opioid antagonist that can reverse fentanyl intoxication by competitively blocking opioid receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which correctly describes the difference between tramadol and morphine?
questions.explanation: Tramadol is a mixed mechanism analgesic with both mu-opioid agonist activity and inhibition of serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake, unlike pure morphine.
options: Tramadol is a mixed opioid–nonopioid analgesic that increases serotonin and norepinephrine, while morphine is a pure opioid agonist
Tramadol is a pure opioid agonist, morphine is mixed
Both act only on μ receptors
Morphine increases serotonin and norepinephrine, tramadol does not
Tramadol has no effect on opioid receptors

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is associated with livedo reticularis as a side effect?
questions.explanation: Amantadine, an antiviral also used in Parkinson's disease, commonly causes livedo reticularis (mottled skin discoloration) as an adverse effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which anti‑Parkinsonian drug commonly produces atropine‑like adverse effects (dry mouth, blurred vision)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine is an anticholinergic anti-Parkinsonian drug that produces peripheral atropine-like side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue therapy to manage sudden episodes of motor deterioration in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is a rapid-acting dopamine agonist used subcutaneously as rescue therapy for sudden off episodes (akinesia) in advanced Parkinson's disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue medication in off akinesia?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine, a dopamine agonist, is used as rescue medication for off akinesia in Parkinson's disease due to its rapid onset when given subcutaneously.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used for tremors (in Parkinson’s)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine (anticholinergic) is particularly effective for tremor in Parkinson's disease, acting by blocking excessive cholinergic activity in the striatum.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug can be used to control tremors in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia?
questions.explanation: Propranolol (beta-blocker) effectively controls essential tremor and is safe in BPH patients, unlike anticholinergics which can cause urinary retention.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Modes of infection in pyogenic meningitis include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pyogenic meningitis spreads via droplet infection, local spread from sinuses, direct implantation (skull fracture), and skin seeding; blood transfusion is NOT a mode.
options: Direct implantation in case of skull fracture

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: CSF in acute septic meningitis does NOT show:
questions.explanation: In acute septic meningitis, CSF shows decreased glucose (bacteria consume it), elevated protein, increased WBCs (neutrophils), and organisms on Gram stain.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: CSF shows cobweb coagulum of fibrin on standing in case of:
questions.explanation: Chronic meningitis causes high protein in CSF leading to fibrin web formation (cobweb coagulum) on standing, unlike acute pyogenic meningitis with diffuse clotting.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cerebellar brain abscess is usually a complication of:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar abscess commonly complicates chronic suppurative otitis media due to direct spread of infection from the middle ear through the tegmen tympani.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Gliosis means:
questions.explanation: Gliosis is the proliferation of astrocytes (astrocytosis) in response to CNS injury, forming a glial scar; it does not involve true tissue regeneration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Infection spreads from suppurative lung diseases to the brain via:
questions.explanation: Infection from suppurative lung diseases (e.g., empyema, lung abscess) spreads to the brain via the vertebral venous plexus (Baton's plexus), which has no valves.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is a:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus (enterovirus), a single-stranded RNA virus that selectively targets motor neurons in the anterior horn.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is usually an infection of:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus specifically infects and destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) of the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis.
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
Posterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mode of infection in poliomyelitis is:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis spreads via the fecal-oral route, primarily through ingestion of contaminated food or water, with feces being the main source of viral shedding.
options: Ingestion of contaminated food or drink
Blood spread from a septic focus

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Muscle paralysis in case of poliomyelitis is due to:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus directly destroys anterior horn motor neurons, leading to denervation of skeletal muscles and subsequent flaccid paralysis without sensory loss.
questions.modelAnswer: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus which selectively targets and destroys the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) of the spinal cord. The destruction of these motor neurons leads to denervation of the corresponding skeletal muscles, resulting in flaccid paralysis. Since the sensory neurons in the posterior horn are spared, there is no sensory loss associated with this paralysis. The extent of paralysis depends on the number and location of motor neurons destroyed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve cell group have same function inside CNS:
questions.explanation: A nucleus is a collection of neuron cell bodies within the CNS that share a common origin and function, such as the red nucleus or substantia nigra.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve group cell outside CNS:
questions.explanation: A ganglion (plural: ganglia) is a collection of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS, such as dorsal root ganglia or autonomic ganglia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve group cell with same origin, function inside CNS:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers with the same origin, course, and termination within the CNS, such as the corticospinal tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve group cell with different origin , function:
questions.explanation: A fasciculus is a compact bundle of fibers having different origins and functions but traveling together, such as the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Crossing of fibers from both sides in middle line:
questions.explanation: Decussation refers to the crossing of nerve fibers from both sides at the midline, such as the pyramidal decussation in the medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ascending sensory bundle in brain stem, end in diencephalon:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus is an ascending sensory bundle in the brainstem carrying fine touch and proprioception information, terminating in the VPL nucleus of thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior column lies between:
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) column lies between the posterior median septum and the posterior horn, carrying proprioception and fine touch sensation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior column lies between:
questions.explanation: The anterior column lies between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neurons for voluntary movement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lateral column lies between:
questions.explanation: The lateral column lies between the anterior and posterior columns, containing ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior column is ........ while lateral, anterior is............
questions.explanation: The posterior column carries only ascending (sensory) fibers, while both lateral and anterior columns contain mixed ascending and descending fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Commissural Nuclei is between:
questions.explanation: Commissural nuclei connect sensory and motor nuclei on opposite sides of the spinal cord, facilitating crossed reflexes and coordinated movement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Central canal in CNS is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal of the CNS is lined by simple cuboidal epithelial cells (ependymal cells), which also line the ventricles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which Nuclei is present in lateral horn?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic (intermediolateral) nucleus is present in the lateral horn at T1-L2 levels, containing preganglionic sympathetic neurons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sympathetic Nuclei is present in:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn from thoracic to upper 2 lumbar segments (T1-L2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior column is present between:
questions.explanation: The anterior column is located between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neuron pools.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Grey matter is .......... While white matter is ...........
questions.explanation: Grey matter (cell bodies) is centrally located in the spinal cord while white matter (myelinated fibers) is peripherally located, the reverse of the brain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of proprioception pathway except:
questions.explanation: Proprioception uses large cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia and thick myelinated fibers, not medium cells with thin unmyelinated fibers.
options: large cell in spinal ganglia, thick unmyleinated nerve fiber
enter CNS from medial division of posterior column of white matter
medium cell in spinal ganglia, thin unmyleinated fiber
long ascending as Gracile , cuneate tract

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: First order Neuron in proprioception path way end in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in the proprioception pathway cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglion; their fibers enter the upper half of the spinal cord and ascend.
options: upper half of spinal cord then ascend as tract

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Second order Neuron start in ........., going via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons start in the medulla (gracile and cuneate nuclei) and cross to form the medial lemniscus, ascending to the thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Third order Neuron start in ......... going via ...........
questions.explanation: Third order neurons in sensory pathways start in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus and project via internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Gracile tract arise from:
questions.explanation: The gracile fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower body (sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the gracile nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cuneate tract arise from:
questions.explanation: The cuneate fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the upper body (cervical and upper thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of medial lemniscus except:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus arises from the upper closed medulla (after crossing as internal arcuate fibers), not from the pons; it carries sensory information to the thalamus.
options: cross from opposite side to thalamus
arise from pons in brain stem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: ........... means sensation of movement, vibration, position
questions.explanation: Proprioception encompasses the sensation of movement (kinesthesia), vibration, and joint/limb position, mediated by muscle spindles, tendon organs, and joint receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: ........... tactile localization, discrimination
questions.explanation: Fine (discriminative) touch enables tactile localization and two-point discrimination, mediated by Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs traveling via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All receptors of proprioception except:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, tendon spindles (Golgi tendon organs), and joint receptors; Merkel discs are tactile receptors, not proprioceptive.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All receptors of fine touch except:
questions.explanation: Fine touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs, and Ruffini endings; tendon spindles are proprioceptive receptors, not tactile.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Gracile, cuneate tract are:
questions.explanation: Gracile and cuneate tracts ascend ipsilaterally in the posterior columns before crossing in the medulla at the sensory decussation.
options: may be same or opposite side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Axon in proprioception ascend in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception fibers from the thalamus ascend via the posterior limb of the internal capsule (along with other sensory fibers) to the primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Receptors of crude touch are:
questions.explanation: Crude (light) touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs combined with free nerve endings, and peritrichial (hair follicle) nerve endings.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of crude touch except:
questions.explanation: Crude touch uses medium-sized cells in dorsal root ganglia (not small), entering via the medial division of the posterior root, and ends in cortex area 3,1,2.
options: medium sized cell in spinal ganglia
enter medial division of posterior root
small sized cell in spinal ganglia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: First order neuron in crude touch end in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons for crude touch have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia; their central processes enter the posterior root and ascend in the posterior column.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Second order neuron starts in ....... goes via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons in the crude touch pathway start in the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus) of the spinal cord and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ventral spinothalamic tract is:
questions.explanation: The ventral spinothalamic tract crosses at the spinal cord level and ascends through the brainstem, eventually reaching the thalamus via the spinal lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Spinal lemniscus made by joining:
questions.explanation: The spinal lemniscus is formed by the union of ventral and lateral spinothalamic tracts, carrying pain and temperature sensation through the brainstem.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Receptors of pain, temperature are:
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are the receptors for pain and temperature sensation throughout the body; they are the most primitive and widely distributed sensory receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of pain, temperature pathway except:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature pathway uses small cells in dorsal root ganglia entering via the lateral division (not medium cells entering medially).
options: enter lateral division of posterior root
medium cell in spinal ganglia that enter medial division of posterior root

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: First order neuron of pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
questions.explanation: First order neurons for pain/temperature are small cells in dorsal root ganglia whose fibers enter via the lateral division of the posterior root and synapse in substantia gelatinosa.
options: small cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
small cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root
medium cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
large cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of lateral spino-thalamic tract except:
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract arises from the opposite side (after crossing in the spinal cord) and ascends through all brainstem levels to the thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Second order neuron in pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for pain/temperature start in the substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) of the posterior horn and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of proprioception pathway of face, head except:
questions.explanation: Facial proprioception uses unipolar neurons (no ganglia) with the mesencephalic nucleus as first order neuron; it is multipolar with proprioceptive ganglia, not sensory.
options: mesencephalic nucleus is first order neuron
main sensory nucleus is second order neuron

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: First order neuron in touch from head face is .............. while second order neuron is ..........
questions.explanation: For facial touch, the first order neuron is in the trigeminal nucleus (mesencephalic for proprioception, principal sensory for touch) and the second order is the main sensory nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: First order neuron in pain, temperature from head face is .............. while second order neuron is ..........
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the face: first order neurons are in the trigeminal (spinal) nucleus, second order are in the spinal trigeminal nucleus that projects to the thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lemniscus of pathway from face and head called:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) carries facial sensory information (touch, pain, temperature) from the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei to the VPM thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of dorsal spinocerebellar tract except:
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb and trunk on the ipsilateral side (after crossing once in the spinal cord via Clarke's nucleus).
options: ascending in white matter then closed medulla then end in cerebellum
carry impulse from lower limb only on same side
carry impulse from lower limb, trunk in opposite side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of ventral spinocerebellar tract except:
questions.explanation: The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb on both sides (decussates twice) and trunk on the same side, not only trunk on same side.
options: ascend in all level of white matter then brain stem
carry impulse from trunk on same side only
carry impulse from lower limb on same or opposite side
arise from cells in posterior horn (V-VII)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Dorsal spinocerebellar enters cerebellum through ............. while ventral spinocerebellar through.............
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle while the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
options: Superior cerebellar peduncle, inferior cerebellar peduncle
inferior cerebellar peduncle, superior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of spino-tectal tract except:
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract arises from posterior horn cells (laminae I, V), ascends contralaterally to the superior colliculus for reflex eye/head movements, not the inferior olivary nucleus.
options: arise from nerve cell in posterior horn (I,V)
ascend at all level of spinal on opposite side then tectum in mid brain
drive reflex, movement of eye, head
ascend in inferior olivary nucleus in medulla

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All characters of spino-olivary tract except:
questions.explanation: The spino-olivary tract ascends to the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to mediate cerebellar climbing fiber input for motor learning, not eye/head reflexes.
options: arise from nerve cell in posterior horn (IV,V)
ascend at all level of spinal on opposite side
drive reflex, movement of eye, head
ascend in inferior olivary nucleus in medulla

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following paired tract except:
questions.explanation: The sulcomarginal tract is a descending motor tract in the anterior column, not a paired bilateral tract like vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and tectospinal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following is single tract except:
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract is a single midline tract (decussates in the midbrain); the other tracts (rubro-spinal, olivo-spinal) are also single but have bilateral components.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following direct tract except:
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal and rubrospinal tracts are indirect (multineuronal) tracts, while olivespinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, and sulcomarginal are direct.
options: ventral reticulo-spinal tract and sulco-marginal tract

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tecto-spinal tract arise from:
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus of the midbrain tectum and descends to control reflexive head and neck movements in response to visual stimuli.
options: superior colliculus of tectum in mid brain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All those tract end in all level of spinal cord except:
questions.explanation: Rubrospinal and ventral vestibulospinal tracts do NOT extend to all spinal levels; lateral vestibulospinal, sulcomarginal, and reticulospinal do.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Molecular layer Contains all the following except:
questions.explanation: The molecular layer contains outer stellate cells, inner basket cells, Purkinje cell dendrites, Golgi cell dendrites, and parallel fibers (Granular cell axons); mossy fibers are in the granular layer.
options: Mossy fiber, dendrite of granular cell

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Primary integrative neuron of cerebral Cortex:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the primary integrative neurons of the cerebellar cortex, receiving input from climbing and parallel fibers and outputting via their axons to deep nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Large pyriform multipolar Cell:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are large pyriform (pear-shaped) multipolar neurons with a characteristic flask-shaped cell body and extensive dendritic tree.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following characters of Golgi Cell except:
questions.explanation: Golgi cells have large cell bodies with many long dendrites that extend into all cortical layers (not just the Golgi layer), and their axons synapse with granular cells in the granular layer.
options: dendrite extend in all cortex layer
its axon in granular layers that synapse with granular cell
its dendrite in golgi layer only

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: -- Contains T-shaped axon in Molecular layer:
questions.explanation: Granular cells have T-shaped axons (parallel fibers) that run tangentially in the molecular layer, forming excitatory synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Purkinje cells are stimulated by the following except:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are excited by climbing fibers, mossy fibers (indirectly via granule cells), and parallel fibers; basket and Golgi cells provide inhibitory input.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cerebral medulla contain all the following except:
questions.explanation: The cerebral medulla contains afferent/efferent fibers, dentate nuclei, and Purkinje fiber axons; Purkinje cells themselves are in the cerebellar cortex, not the medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle continue in spinal cord through:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus continues in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal and sulcomarginal tracts, coordinating head-eye movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Border cell attached by:
questions.explanation: Border cells (meningothelial cells) between arachnoid and dura are attached by both tight junctions and desmosomes for structural integrity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Leptomeninges is membrane between:
questions.explanation: Leptomeninges refers to the pia mater and arachnoid mater together, which are delicate membranes lying between the dura mater and subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One layer of modified fibroblast:
questions.explanation: The pia mater consists of a single layer of modified fibroblasts (mesothelial cells) that closely follow the contours of the brain and spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: -- present between extracerebral capillary, subarachnoid space:
questions.explanation: The arachnoid barrier cell layer is present between extracerebral capillaries and the subarachnoid space, regulating CSF composition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Blood brain barrier formed of all the following except:
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier consists of thick basement membrane, non-fenestrated endothelium, and astrocyte foot processes; ependymal cells form the CSF barrier, not BBB.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Type of junction between endothelium or ependymal:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between endothelial cells and ependymal cells create the selective permeability barrier in the CNS.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood CSF barrier is formed of all the following except:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by endothelial cells, basement membrane, and ependymal cells with tight junctions; astrocyte foot processes are part of the BBB, not blood-CSF barrier.
options: endothelial cells of the blood capillaries
basement membrane of the blood capillaries
ependymal cells that are connected by tight junctions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood brain barrier is formed of all the following except:
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier consists of endothelial cells, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes; ependymal cells with tight junctions form the ventricular lining, not the BBB.
options: basement membrane of the blood capillaries
ependymal cells that are connected by tight junctions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The central nervous system is soft because:
questions.explanation: The CNS lacks connective tissue (except at surfaces), making it soft; this also explains its vulnerability to mechanical injury.
options: It consists of neurons joined by connective tissue.
It is rich in blood vessels.
It does not contain connective tissue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Grey matter is central in spinal cord with neuron cell bodies; white matter is peripheral with myelinated fibers; the CNS lacks connective tissue framework.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers; the distribution depends on myelin location.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells) that is partially ciliated, similar to the ventricular lining.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated fibers; myelinated nerve fibers are found in white matter.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Lumbar level has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it has relatively less white matter (fewer descending motor fibers passing through).
options: Smallest white matter / grey matter ratio.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of thoracic level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Thoracic spinal cord has lateral horns (intermediolateral cell columns) containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons, giving it 4 horns.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains the most descending and ascending fibers passing to/from the brain.
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following tracts carries sensations to subcortical level:
questions.explanation: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum (subcortical level); other tracts listed go to thalamus/cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors (Pacinian corpuscles at joints), providing limb position sense.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a receptor for vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic lamellar structure in the dermis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in proprioception from the lower body have cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia) at corresponding levels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the upper half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in proprioception from the upper body also have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia), same as lower body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The second order neuron in proprioception from lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for lower body proprioception are in the gracile nucleus on the same side, which then decussates as internal arcuate fibers.
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibres are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (second order proprioceptive neurons crossing) are present in the closed medulla where the gracile and cuneate nuclei are located.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: External arcuate fibres carry impulses to:
questions.explanation: External arcuate fibers carry proprioceptive and vestibular information to the cerebellum via the peduncles, forming the mossy fiber input.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is true about gracile tract:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract carries proprioception from the lower half of the body (sacral, lumbar, lower thoracic) and terminates in the gracile nucleus of the medulla.
options: Presents only in cervical & thoracic levels of spinal cord.
Carries proprioception from the upper half of the body.
Terminates at gracile nucleus in medulla.
Arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is true about cuneate tract:
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia in the upper half of the body (cervical and upper thoracic) and carries upper limb proprioception.
options: It arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on same side.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on opposite side.
It is present in lateral column of white matter in spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior external arcuate fibres connect:
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior external arcuate fibres connect:
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior external arcuate fibres relay in:
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the arcuate nucleus of the opposite side before projecting to the cerebellum.
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arcuate fibres carry:
questions.explanation: Arcuate fibers (both internal and external) carry proprioceptive impulses from the body to the cerebellum and brainstem nuclei.
options: Pain and temperature from the head.
Pain and temperature from the body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibres:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the medulla, cross at the sensory decussation, and form the medial lemniscus.
options: Arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Terminate at gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Carry proprioceptive impulses from the head.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of medial lemniscus is:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus originates from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side after their fibers cross (internal arcuate fibers).
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of same side.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of opposite side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Decussation of internal arcuate fibres takes place in:
questions.explanation: Decussation of internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) occurs in the upper part of the closed medulla, at the level of the olivary nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is true about first order neurons in proprioception of the body:
questions.explanation: First order proprioceptive neurons have large cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia with thick myelinated fibers that give off ascending and descending branches in the posterior column.
options: They are the small cells in spinal ganglia.
They have thin unmyelinated nerve fibres.
Their central branches enter the spinal cord through the lateral division of the posterior roots.
They give ascending and descending branches in spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes form the blood-brain barrier through their foot processes surrounding CNS capillaries, regulating molecular passage into the brain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following statements is true:
questions.explanation: The ventral vestibulospinal tract passes in the medial longitudinal bundle, coordinating head position and eye movements.
options: 20% of the pyramidal fibers cross in pyramidal decussation.
The first order neuron for proprioception from head is in spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve.
The ventral vestibulospinal tract passes in medial longitudinal bundle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first order neurons in proprioception pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains first order neurons for proprioception from the face, the only case of sensory neurons in the CNS.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first order neurons for pain and temperature pathway from face and head are located in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons for pain and temperature from the face have cell bodies in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, with central processes entering the spinal nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The second order neuron in simple touch pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for simple touch from the face are in the main (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Trigeminal lemniscus is present in:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) is present in the medulla and pons, carrying facial sensory information to the VPM thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The final neurons in the auditory pathway are cells of:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body contains the final neurons of the auditory pathway, projecting via the acoustic radiation to the primary auditory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arachnoid barrier is the barrier between:
questions.explanation: The arachnoid barrier cell layer separates extracerebral capillaries from the subarachnoid space, contributing to the blood-CSF barrier.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier at the ventricular surface, along with choroid plexus epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Blood brain barrier is formed of tight junctions between:
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier uses tight junctions between non-fenestrated (continuous) capillary endothelial cells, unlike fenestrated endothelium elsewhere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Border cells can be found in:
questions.explanation: Border cells (meningothelial cells) are found in the arachnoid mater, forming a continuous layer adjacent to the dura.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesothelial cells), a single layer that closely invests the brain and spinal cord surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is true about climbing fibres:
questions.explanation: Each climbing fiber forms powerful excitatory synapses with multiple Purkinje cell dendrites; one Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber.
options: Each fibre synapse with one Purkinje cell.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If a patient cannot recognize an unseen familiar object placed in his hand, the sensory tract that might be affected is:
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of objects by touch) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway; cuneate tract carries this from the upper limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl diagnosed with meningitis. The doctor prescribes her antibiotics. Which of the following statements should be considered true?
questions.explanation: In meningitis, inflamed meninges become more permeable allowing increased penicillin entry; normal BBB restricts many antibiotics from CNS.
options: The blood brain barrier normally allows the passage of all antibiotics.
The blood brain barrier does not allow the passage of antibiotics due to their big molecular size.
The systemic administration of penicillin normally results in large amount entering CNS.
The meninges become more permeable to penicillin at the site of inflammation and its concentration rises in cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with lesion in the right gracile nucleus is expected to have diminished:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the right gracile nucleus impairs fine touch and stereognosis on the right lower limb (ipsilateral) because the gracile tract is already ipsilateral.
options: tactile localization at the right arm
fine touch at the left leg
tactile discrimination at the right leg

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An injury to the posterior column of the lumbar spinal cord may be manifested as loss of:
questions.explanation: Posterior column lesion at lumbar level causes loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (tactile discrimination) in the ipsilateral lower limbs.
options: fine touch at the upper limbs.
tactile discrimination at the lower limbs
crude touch at the upper limbs
pain & temperature at the lower limbs

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following can be found in a patient diagnosed with syringomyelia?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution over upper limbs and chest.
options: loss of pain and temperature in the upper limbs and chest.
loss of touch in the upper limbs and chest
loss of pain and temperature in the abdomen and lower limbs
loss of touch in the abdomen and lower limbs

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with defective pain, temperature, simple touch and proprioception sensations from one side of the face and scalp probably has lesion in:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus carries all sensory modalities from one side of the face; lesion causes contralateral facial sensory loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Examination of the lower limbs in a patient diagnosed with tabes dorsalis can reveal one of the following:
questions.explanation: Tabes dorsalis (dorsal column degeneration in neurosyphilis) causes sensory ataxia due to loss of proprioception, leading to gait problems.
options: bilateral loss of pain and temperature

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the lateral ventricle, choose one correct answer:
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricle is the only cavity in the telencephalon, with anterior horn in frontal lobe, body in parietal, and posterior/temporal horns in temporal lobe.
options: Its anterior horn lies in the parietal lobe.
Its posterior horn lies in the temporal lobe.
Is the only cavity in the telencephalon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the cerebrospinal fluid, choose one correct answer:
questions.explanation: The third ventricle has choroid plexus in its roof (derived from tela choroidea) producing CSF; lateral ventricles also have choroid plexus.
options: Produced mainly in the subarachnoid space.
Third ventricle has a choroid plexus in its roof.
Fourth ventricle has a choroid plexus in its floor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the choroid plexus; choose one best answer:
questions.explanation: Choroid plexus is formed by a capillary network (from pia) covered by a thin layer of cuboidal epithelial cells (modified ependyma).
options: Is formed by a plexus of capillaries and a thin layer of cuboidal epithelium.
Is responsible for absorption of the cerebrospinal fluid.
All of the choroids plexuses are present in the floor of the ventricles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the fourth ventricle; choose the most correct answer:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
options: Its floor is formed by the closed medulla and pons.
Its roof is formed by the superior and inferior medullary vela.
Its choroids plexus is present in the floor of the ventricle.
It has a communication with the lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following structures is a content of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The optic tract is a content of the interpeduncular fossa, carrying visual information from the optic chiasma to the lateral geniculate body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the interpeduncular fossa, one of the following is a boundary of the fossa:
questions.explanation: The optic tract forms the lateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa; the cerebral peduncles form the posterior boundary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is correct:
questions.explanation: Olfactory nerve filaments from the nasal mucosa synapse in the olfactory bulb, which then projects via the olfactory tract to cortical areas.
options: The anterior perforated substance lies on the medial side of the optic chiasma.
The olfactory nerve filaments end in the olfactory bulb.
The lateral olfactory root ends in the cuneus.
The infundibulum connects the tuber cinereum with the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following cranial nerves contains sensory nerves fibers:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) contains sensory fibers for face, scalp, and oral cavity; the other listed nerves are purely motor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following cranial nerves is attached to the posterior aspect of the brain stem:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the posterior aspect of the brainstem, specifically from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cisterna magna of subarachnoid space is a name given to the:
questions.explanation: The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern located between the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the cerebellum, choose one correct answer:
questions.explanation: The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) regulates muscle tone and coordination; the neocerebellum plans movement and the paleocerebellum controls equilibrium.
options: Middle cerebellar peduncle connects it to medulla oblongata.
Paleocerebellum is concerned with planning and programming movement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) the lesion is in one of the following arteries:
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient shows definite weakness of the right facial muscles while facial skin sensation is normal. On testing of the ocular movements, there is evidence of slight weakness of the right lateral rectus muscle. Radiology reveals the presence of tumour. Locate the possible site of the tumour.
questions.explanation: Inferior pons lesion affecting CN VI nucleus causes facial weakness (CN VII) and lateral rectus weakness (CN VI), with normal sensation pointing to a pontine tumor.
options: Closed medulla at level of motor decussation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient complains of tremors in the right hand while doing fine movements. When asked to walk along a straight line on the floor, the patient sways over to the right side. When asked to touch his nose with his right index finger, the right hand displays tremor, and the finger tends to overshoot the target. At surgery, he is found to have tumour. Locate the possible site of tumour.
questions.explanation: Intention tremor, overshoot (dysmetria), and swaying to the right during gait indicate a right cerebellar lesion; the tumor is in the right cerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A female patient has reduced pain and temperature sense in upper limbs and chest but her sense of tactile discrimination is perfectly normal in these areas. State which tract/tracts is/are involved and name the disease.
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved tactile discrimination.
options: Lateral spinothalamic and gracile – Tabes dorsalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neurologist observes a patient with a high stamping gait. He asks the patient to stand and to close his eyes. The patient immediately starts to sway over. Name the ascending pathways that are involved and name the disease.
questions.explanation: Bilateral gracile tract degeneration in tabes dorsalis causes loss of proprioception leading to sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign (swaying with eyes closed).
options: Gracile on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Gracile on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with proximal, jerky, non‑purposeful movements of the limbs accompanied by hypotonia. Degeneration of which central nervous system structure is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Chorea (jerky, non-purposeful movements) with hypotonia results from caudate nucleus degeneration in Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition.
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 52‑year‑old man has had progressive headaches and concentration difficulties for two months. His behaviour becomes odd, and he then suffers a generalised seizure. MRI shows a large, necrotic mass in the left cerebral hemisphere that crosses the corpus callosum into the right hemisphere. Which neoplasm is most likely?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme typically crosses the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma), shows necrosis and ring enhancement, and has poor prognosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 23‑year‑old man is found unconscious after a fall. CT shows a biconvex, lens‑shaped hyperdensity between the skull and the dura. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation: A biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdensity between skull and dura is an epidural hematoma, typically from traumatic middle meningeal artery rupture.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn boy has an underdeveloped mandible and zygomatic bone, low‑set slanting eyes, and facial asymmetry. Which pharyngeal arch is most likely defective?
questions.explanation: First pharyngeal arch derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and muscles of mastication; defect causes Treacher Collins-like features.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 10‑year‑old girl has a cystic cerebellar tumour. Microscopy shows spindle cells with hair‑like processes, microcysts, and Rosenthal fibres. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma in children shows characteristic hair-like processes (ROSE), microcysts, and Rosenthal fibers; often cystic with mural nodule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 28‑year‑old woman has unilateral tinnitus, vertigo, and progressive hearing loss. MRI reveals a 3 cm mass at the cerebellopontine angle. Which microscopic finding is most characteristic?
questions.explanation: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at cerebellopontine angle shows Antoni A (cellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular) areas with verocay bodies.
options: Whorled spindle cells with psammoma bodies
Hypo‑ and hypercellular areas (Antoni A and B)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 5‑year‑old boy has recent‑onset gait instability and ataxia. MRI shows a midline posterior fossa mass. Biopsy reveals sheets of primitive small round cells with many mitoses. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most common?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma shows loss of chromosome 17p; it's a small round blue cell tumor of the posterior fossa in children.
options: Loss of the short arm of chromosome 17 (17p)
Loss of the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32‑year‑old woman has difficulty writing, right arm weakness, and reduced light touch on the left leg. CSF shows elevated IgG, mononuclear cells, and oligoclonal bands. Which pathologic finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis shows perivascular lymphocytic cuffing with demyelinated axons in white matter and oligoclonal IgG bands in CSF.
options: Perivascular lymphocytes with demyelinated axons in white matter
Multinucleated cells in grey and white matter

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 56‑year‑old man with polycystic kidney disease develops sudden severe headache and nuchal rigidity. CT shows subarachnoid haemorrhage. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, associated with polycystic kidney disease and autosomal dominant inheritance, is the most common cause of spontaneous SAH.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32‑year‑old woman has right arm weakness and reduced light touch on the left leg. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis presents with oligoclonal bands in CSF, periventricular white matter lesions, and relapsing-remitting neurological deficits.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which part of the anterior wall of the third ventricle is formed by a thin membrane derived from the telencephalon?
questions.explanation: The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle; it is a thin membrane derived from the telencephalon containing the organum vasculosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are constituents of the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus except:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus floor, not the lateral wall; oculomotor, trochlear, V1, and V2 are in the lateral wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which cranial nerve emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla oblongata between the pyramid and the olive?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla between the pyramid and olive, carrying only motor fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The internal arcuate fibres are axons of which nucleus?
