questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of the cuneate and gracile nuclei that cross at the sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Unconscious proprioception from the biceps brachii is carried primarily by which tract?
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract carries proprioception from the upper limb (including biceps brachii) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus of the medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract is responsible for spino‑visual reflexes (turning the head and eyes toward a cutaneous stimulus)?
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following structures wind around the cerebral peduncle except:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve does not wind around the cerebral peduncle; optic tract, trochlear nerve, posterior cerebral artery, and basal vein do.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure is present at the level of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The facial colliculus is formed by:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by the abducens nucleus, around which the facial nerve fibers loop.
options: Motor fibres of the facial nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in its:
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in the inferior roof (posterior medullary velum), not the floor or superior roof.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The median part of the upper lip (philtrum) is derived embryologically from the:
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (from medial nasal prominences) forms the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate, and the four incisor teeth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lateral part of the upper lip is derived from the:
questions.explanation: The lateral upper lip derives from the maxillary prominence (branchial arch 1), along with the lateral cheek and most of the upper lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn has an underdeveloped mandible, zygomatic bone, and low‑set ears. Which pharyngeal arch is defective?
questions.explanation: First pharyngeal arch defect (Treacher Collins syndrome) causes underdeveloped mandible, zygomatic bones, and low-set ears.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini develops from the first pharyngeal arch, innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The branchial arch supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the third branchial arch, which gives rise to stylopharyngeus muscle and the stylotympanic fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptor is specialised for tactile discrimination and two‑point discrimination?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae detect fine touch, texture, and two-point discrimination; they adapt rapidly and are numerous in fingertips.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptor helps a blind person read Braille by detecting fine texture and edges?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles detect fine tactile details and edges, enabling blind individuals to read Braille through subtle texture differences.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The plexus of Bonnet is best described as:
questions.explanation: The plexus of Bonnet (hair follicle receptor network) is a mechanoreceptor formed by free nerve endings that wrap around hair follicles to detect hair movement.
options: A capsulated receptor with concentric lamellae

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptors are located most deeply in the skin (dermis and hypodermis)?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings are the deepest tactile receptors, located in the dermis and hypodermis for vibration and stretch detection.
options: Krause end bulb and free nerve endings

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptor has a motor efferent supply?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers with gamma motor neuron innervation that adjusts sensitivity, unlike other receptors listed which are purely sensory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Golgi tendon organ differs from the muscle spindle in that it:
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs lack gamma motor innervation (unlike muscle spindles), are in series with muscle, and detect tension; both have capsules.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which lamina of the spinal cord corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa?
questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the posterior horn, specializing in pain and temperature modulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Clark’s nucleus (dorsal nucleus) is located in which lamina?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is located in Rexed lamina VII at T1-L2 levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Gamma motor neurons are found in which lamina of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons are located in Rexed lamina IX of the anterior horn, innervating intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a spinal cord lesion has loss of vibration and position sense in both legs but normal pain and temperature sensation. Which tract is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Bilateral loss of vibration and position sense with preserved pain/temperature indicates gracile tract lesion, as it carries proprioception and vibration from the legs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The reticular activating system (RAS) is best described by which statement?
questions.explanation: The RAS receives sensory input from proprioceptors and various sensory modalities to maintain cortical arousal and alertness.
options: Its neurons are located only in the medulla oblongata.
Its neurons can be activated by sensory signals from proprioceptors.
Its activity is decreased by stress.
It discharges inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which EEG wave pattern indicates deep (slow‑wave) sleep in an adult?
questions.explanation: Delta waves (0.5-2 Hz, high amplitude) are the hallmark of deep slow-wave sleep in adults, replacing alpha rhythms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Operant conditioning is a type of:
questions.explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is associative learning where behavior is modified by its consequences (reward or punishment).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Stimulation of the lateral hypothalamic area in an experimental animal produces:
questions.explanation: The lateral hypothalamus is the feeding (hunger) center; stimulation produces hunger and eating behavior, while destruction causes anorexia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Semantic memory refers to:
questions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general facts, concepts, and knowledge independent of personal experience (declarative/explicit memory).
options: Memory of facts and general knowledge

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The representational (non‑dominant) hemisphere in most people is described by which feature?
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere in most people lies in the right hemisphere and is specialized for spatial and holistic processing.
options: It is responsible for language comprehension.
It always lies in the left hemisphere.
It is concerned with analytical tasks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that increases the permeability of the postsynaptic membrane to which ion?
questions.explanation: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels; chloride influx hyperpolarizes the neuron, causing inhibition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The endogenous analgesia system includes which brain region?
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal grey (PAG) in the midbrain contains endogenous opioid neurons that activate descending pain inhibition pathways.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fast pain (first pain) is transmitted to the CNS by which fibres?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers (myelinated, fast-conducting) transmit first/quick pain, while C fibers (unmyelinated) transmit slow, throbbing second pain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following inhibits pain sensation?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibition pathways, reducing pain transmission at the spinal cord level.
options: Activation of the lateral spinothalamic tract

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the cotton wool test for crude touch, the receptors responsible are:
questions.explanation: Mechanoreceptors detect the light touch sensation tested by cotton wool; they include Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tactile discrimination (two‑point discrimination) is best tested by:
questions.explanation: Weber's two-point compass test assesses tactile discrimination ability, testing the spatial resolution of Meissner and Merkel receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiepileptic drug is associated with the highest risk of neonatal cleft lip and cleft palate?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome causing cleft lip/palate, digital hypoplasia, and growth retardation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue medication for sudden akinetic episodes (off‑periods) in advanced Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine (subcutaneous dopamine agonist) is used as rescue therapy for sudden off-periods in advanced Parkinson's disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Antipsychotic‑induced akathisia is best treated with:
questions.explanation: Propranolol (beta-blocker) is first-line treatment for antipsychotic-induced akathisia, likely by blocking beta-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The mood stabiliser with delayed onset, narrow therapeutic index, and requirement for blood level monitoring is:
questions.explanation: Lithium has delayed onset (weeks), narrow therapeutic index (0.6-1.2 mEq/L), and requires regular serum level monitoring.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which combination of drugs should be avoided because both can cause agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine and carbamazepine both cause agranulocytosis; their combination dramatically increases this risk and is contraindicated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiepileptic is used as migraine prophylaxis and can cause weight loss and renal stones?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is used for migraine prophylaxis and causes weight loss and renal calcium phosphate stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antidepressant is approved for management of chronic neuropathic pain (e.g., diabetic neuropathy)?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine (SNRI) and duloxetine are antidepressants approved for diabetic neuropathy and other chronic pain conditions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which statement about ester local anesthetics is false?
questions.explanation: Ester local anesthetics are MORE liable to cause allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite, not less.
options: They are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases.
Procaine is a member of this group.
They are shorter acting than amides.
They are less liable to induce allergy.
They are less liable to systemic toxicity than amides.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The only medically justified long‑term use of phenobarbital is for:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital is justified long-term only for certain epilepsies (generalized tonic-clonic, partial seizures) due to its side effect profile.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The main benefit of adding carbidopa to levodopa in Sinemet is that carbidopa:
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, preventing peripheral levodopa conversion and increasing CNS availability.
options: Inhibits peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which opioid antagonist is also used to reduce alcohol craving?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone (opioid antagonist) is used in alcohol dependence treatment by blocking opioid receptors involved in the rewarding effects of alcohol.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The potency of inhaled anaesthetics is quantitatively defined as the:
questions.explanation: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) defines potency as the alveolar concentration that prevents movement in 50% of patients to a surgical stimulus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiviral drug is used to treat neonates with herpes simplex virus encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir (guanine analog) is the treatment of choice for HSV encephalitis in neonates, reducing mortality when given early.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An important virulence factor of *Cryptococcus neoformans* is the production of:
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans produces melanin via phenol oxidase, which protects against oxidative stress and is a major virulence factor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The vaccine used for protection against tetanus consists of:
questions.explanation: Tetanus vaccine contains inactivated tetanus toxin (toxoid) that stimulates antibody production without causing disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which characteristic is true of *Listeria monocytogenes*?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
options: It is strictly a human pathogen.
It can grow at refrigerator temperature (4°C).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a suspected case of rabies, the most important specimen for virus detection is:
questions.explanation: Saliva contains the highest concentration of rabies virus; a skin biopsy from the nape of the neck (hair follicles) is also used for fluorescent antibody testing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is a cannabinoid drug used for management of hashish (cannabis) dependence?
questions.explanation: Dronabinol (synthetic THC) is used medically for cannabis dependence, providing agonist effects that reduce withdrawal and craving.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the urea cycle, which two compounds are end products (released from the cycle)?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which enzyme is stimulated by cortisol to increase epinephrine synthesis?
questions.explanation: PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by cortisol in the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which cofactor is required for the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; BH4 deficiency causes PKU.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The inborn error of branched‑chain amino acid metabolism that causes a burnt‑sugar odour in urine is:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine with characteristic sweet odor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a coenzyme for the oxidative decarboxylation of:
questions.explanation: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids including pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain ketoacids.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death) is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, classically presenting with the 4 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which vitamin is directly involved in one‑carbon transfer reactions (e.g., purine and thymidylate synthesis)?
questions.explanation: Folate (as N5, N10-methylene-THF) donates one-carbon units in purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Methyl‑THF donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form:
questions.explanation: Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following releases free ammonia in the body?
questions.explanation: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP are allosteric activators of glutamate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is activated by:
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate) is the essential allosteric activator of CPS I, the first urea cycle enzyme.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which compound links the urea cycle with the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: Fumarate links the urea and citric acid cycles; it is produced from argininosuccinate in the urea cycle and enters the CAC.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Serotonin is synthesised from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The central nervous system is soft because it:
questions.explanation: The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood‑CSF barrier is NOT formed by:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier uses fenestrated endothelial cells (allowing passage) and is NOT formed by astrocyte foot processes (those form the BBB).
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junctions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle (midbrain) would present with:
questions.explanation: Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
options: Loss of fine touch on the left side of the body
Loss of pain sensation on the right side
Skeletal motor loss on the entire left side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the 2 enlargements present in the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3) enlargements for limb innervation, corresponding to brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical enlargement and lumbar enlargement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Compare between the spinal cord of the adult and the newborn:
questions.explanation: In adults the spinal cord extends from C1 to L1 vertebra, while in newborns it extends from C1 to L3 vertebra due to differential vertebral column growth.
questions.modelAnswer: Adult: C1 till L1; Newborn: C1 till L3.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the 3 ligaments supporting the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments supporting the spinal cord are the filum terminale (coccygeal ligament), ligamentum denticulatum, and subarachnoid septum.
questions.modelAnswer: Filum terminale, ligamentum denticulatum, subarachnoid septum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete: Dura
questions.explanation: The dura mater and arachnoid mater (the meninges) end opposite the S2 vertebra, forming the sacral dural sac.
questions.modelAnswer: mater and arachnoid mater end opposite which vertebrae? S2

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Extent of the scalp:
questions.explanation: The scalp extends from the supraorbital margin anteriorly to the external occipital protuberance posteriorly, and to the superior temporal line laterally.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: supraorbital margin; Posteriorly: external occipital protuberance and highest nuchal line; Laterally: superior temporal line.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Effects of dense connective tissue in scalp:
questions.explanation: Dense connective tissue in the scalp means infections remain localized, wounds gape less due to fibrous septa, and small wounds cause profuse bleeding from arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Infection remains localized, wounds don't gap, small wound causes profuse bleeding.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Compare frontal and occipital belly nerve supply:
questions.explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis is innervated by the temporal branch of facial nerve; the occipital belly is innervated by the posterior auricular branch.
questions.modelAnswer: Frontal belly: temporal branch of facial nerve; Occipital belly: posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Why is loose connective tissue the dangerous layer?
questions.explanation: The loose areolar tissue (dangerous layer) contains valveless emissary veins connecting scalp veins to intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection spread.
questions.modelAnswer: Because its emissary veins can spread infection from scalp to cranial cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sensory nerve supply of scalp:
questions.explanation: Anterior to auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal nerves; posterior to auricle: great auricular, lesser/greater occipital, third occipital.
questions.modelAnswer: In front of auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal; Behind auricle: great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital, third occipital.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of face:
questions.explanation: The face is bounded superiorly by the hairline, inferiorly by the lower mandibular border, and laterally by the auricles connecting both sides.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: hair line; Inferior: lower border of mandible; Sideways: from one auricle to the other.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Facial artery terminates by anastomosing with:
questions.explanation: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery, completing the arterial supply around the eye and nose.
questions.modelAnswer: Dorsal nasal artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 2 branches of facial artery in face:
questions.explanation: The two terminal branches of the facial artery within the face are the superior labial artery and inferior labial artery supplying the lips.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior labial and Inferior labial.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Deep communications of anterior facial vein:
questions.explanation: The anterior facial vein communicates deeply with the superior ophthalmic vein (to cavernous sinus) and deep facial vein (to pterygoid plexus).
questions.modelAnswer: To superior ophthalmic vein (→ cavernous sinus) and to deep facial vein (→ pterygoid venous plexus → cavernous sinus via emissary veins).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Dangerous area of face:
questions.explanation: The dangerous area of the face (midline triangle including upper lip and nose) connects via angular/emissary veins to the cavernous sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Triangle including upper lip, nose, medial angles of eye. Infection can spread to cavernous sinus causing thrombosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of ophthalmic nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches in the face include supratrochlear, supraorbital (from frontal nerve), and infratrochlear nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: Supratrochlear, supraorbital, palpebral branch of lacrimal, infratrochlear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off infraorbital, zygomatic, and greater palatine nerves in the face, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper teeth.
questions.modelAnswer: Infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, greater palatine nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 branches of infraorbital nerve:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of V2) gives inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, and anterior superior alveolar branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, anterior superior alveolar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Branches of mandibular nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) gives mental and auriculotemporal branches on the face; the motor branches (masseteric, temporal, buccal) supply muscles of mastication.
questions.modelAnswer: Mental nerve (from inferior alveolar), auriculotemporal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Muscles of facial expression develop from:
questions.explanation: Muscles of facial expression develop from the second pharyngeal arch (hyoid arch), innervated by CN VII (facial nerve).
questions.modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch mesoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of first somatosensory area causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the first somatosensory area (S1, postcentral gyrus) causes contralateral loss of fine touch, pressure, and stereognosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral loss of fine touch, pressure, and stereognosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of first somatosensory area:
questions.explanation: The first somatosensory area is located in the postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2) of the parietal lobe, posterior to the central sulcus.
questions.modelAnswer: Postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2) of parietal lobe.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of second somatosensory area:
questions.explanation: The second somatosensory area (S2) is located in the superior wall of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), deep to the parietal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior wall of lateral sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of area 43:
questions.explanation: Area 43 (taste cortex) is located in the lower part of the postcentral gyrus near the insula, where gustatory and general sensation integrate.
questions.modelAnswer: Lower postcentral gyrus adjacent to operculum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of areas 5 & 7 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of areas 5 and 7 (superior parietal lobule) causes sensory neglect of contralateral side, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory neglect, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of inferior parietal lobule:
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule (areas 40, 39) is located below the intraparietal sulcus, behind the lateral sulcus, comprising supramarginal and angular gyri.
questions.modelAnswer: Below intraparietal sulcus, consisting of angular and supramarginal gyri.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of inferior parietal lobule causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule causes Gerstmann syndrome (left lesion): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
questions.modelAnswer: Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 speech centers:
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech), Wernicke's area (comprehension), and the arcuate fasciculus connecting them.
questions.modelAnswer: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, arcuate fasciculus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of primary motor area:
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (M1) is located in the precentral gyrus (area 4) of the frontal lobe, anterior to the central sulcus.
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus (area 4) of frontal lobe.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Body representation of premotor area:
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) has a somatotopic representation similar to M1, controlling proximal and trunk muscles with less discrete localization.
questions.modelAnswer: Similar to motor cortex but controls proximal muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of area 4 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes spastic paralysis of contralateral muscles with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski sign.
questions.modelAnswer: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign on contralateral side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of premotor area:
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located anterior to the precentral gyrus on the lateral and medial surfaces of the frontal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior to precentral gyrus on lateral and medial frontal lobe.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of area 6 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 6 (premotor area) causes loss of skilled movement, motor apraxia, and rigidity without true paralysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Motor apraxia, loss of skilled movement, rigidity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of frontal eye field:
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) is located in the middle frontal gyrus anterior to the premotor area, controlling voluntary eye movements.
questions.modelAnswer: Middle frontal gyrus, anterior to premotor area.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of area 8 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 8 (frontal eye field) causes conjugate deviation of eyes toward the side of the lesion (inability to look away).
questions.modelAnswer: Conjugate eye deviation toward the lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area (speech apraxia) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of the dominant hemisphere, usually the left.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of dominant hemisphere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Lesion of Broca's area causes expressive (motor) aphasia: non-fluent speech with good comprehension but impaired repetition.
questions.modelAnswer: Expressive aphasia: non-fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Site of supplementary motor area:
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located on the medial surface of the frontal lobe anterior to the leg area of M1.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial frontal lobe above area 4.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of SMA causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of SMA causes loss of spontaneous movement, speech initiation, and bilateral motor planning without paralysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Loss of spontaneous movement and speech initiation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 neurons for pain and temperature from body:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the body uses three neurons: DRG (pseudounipolar), substantia gelatinosa (second order), VPL thalamus (third order).
questions.modelAnswer: First order: dorsal root ganglion; Second order: substantia gelatinosa; Third order: VPL thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 neurons for pain and temperature from face:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from face: first order in trigeminal ganglion, second order in spinal trigeminal nucleus, third order in VPM thalamus.
questions.modelAnswer: First order: trigeminal ganglion; Second order: spinal trigeminal nucleus; Third order: VPM thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 neurons for crude touch and pressure:
questions.explanation: Crude touch uses three neurons: DRG (first), nucleus proprius (second), VPL thalamus (third), ascending via anterior spinothalamic tract.
questions.modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: nucleus proprius; Third order: VPL thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sensations carried:
questions.explanation: Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception sensations are carried by the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway to the somatosensory cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 neurons for conscious proprioception and fine touch:
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception uses three neurons: DRG (first order), gracile/cuneate nuclei (second order, crossing in medulla), VPL thalamus (third order), via medial lemniscus to cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: gracile/cuneate nuclei; Third order: VPL thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 4 tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The four tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to cerebellum are dorsal spinocerebellar, ventral spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and rostral spinocerebellar tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: Dorsal spinocerebellar, ventral spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, rostral spinocerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tract forming external arcuate fibers:
questions.explanation: The external arcuate fibers arise from the cuneate nucleus and carry proprioceptive information to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: Cuneate nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tracts carrying unconscious proprioception from lower limb:
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb is carried by the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus) to the cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract and ventral spinocerebellar tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 2 extrapyramidal tracts:
questions.explanation: The two main extrapyramidal tracts are the reticulospinal tract (medial and lateral) and the vestibulospinal tract (lateral and medial).
questions.modelAnswer: Rubro-spinal tract and vestibulo-spinal tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Origin of olivospinal tract:
questions.explanation: The olivospinal tract arises from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla and descends to the spinal cord to influence motor activity.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lamination of lateral corticospinal tract in spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract is laminated: cervical fibers are most lateral, sacral fibers most medial, controlling progressive distal-to-proximal muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical fibers most lateral, sacral most medial.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lamination of pyramidal tract in internal capsule:
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract is arranged: anterior limb (frontal connections), genu (face), posterior limb (arm, leg) from front to back.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior limb: frontal; Genu: face; Posterior limb: arm above, leg below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tracts ending on alpha and gamma neurons of extensors:
questions.explanation: Extensor muscles are controlled by lateral vestibulospinal (facilitates extensors) and medial reticulospinal tracts via gamma neurons.
questions.modelAnswer: Vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete: Tectospinal
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus, decussates, and descends to control reflex head/neck movements toward visual stimuli.
questions.modelAnswer: Origin: superior colliculus; Function: reflex head and neck movements toward visual stimuli.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 arteries supplying spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three arteries supplying the spinal cord are the anterior spinal artery (ventral median spinal artery) and two posterior spinal arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: One anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Artery supplying medial medulla and anterior 2/3 of spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla and anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the corticospinal tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery.
